summary: During a first-fruits festival God renews the covenant, renames Abram and Sarai, promises Sarah a son called Isaac, and commands circumcision of the household on the eighth day. The angel then extends the rule to Israel, distinguishes Isaac's line from Ishmael and Esau, and warns that future generations may neglect the sign.
whyItMatters: The chapter defines belonging through a bodily covenant sign and the promised line of Isaac, while its severe exclusionary language requires careful reading in its own ancient setting.

context.author: Within the book, the angel of the presence dictates the account to Moses; the historical writer is unnamed.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through Moses in the book’s frame; the specific first historical audience is not identified.
context.date: The narrative places the revelation at Sinai; the historical Hebrew work is usually dated to the second century BCE, without an established exact year.
context.setting: Abraham's household during a festival and the Sinai instruction addressed to Israel about the covenant sign.
context.literaryForm: Covenant dialogue followed by ritual ordinance and an angelic warning.

before.text: The previous chapter promised Abram descendants despite childlessness, and Hagar bore Ishmael.

here.text: Abraham and Sarah receive new names, Isaac is promised, and circumcision becomes the household covenant sign.

after.text: The following chapter narrates Sarah’s promised pregnancy and birth of Isaac alongside judgment on Sodom.

outline.heading: Festival and renewal of the covenant
outline.note: Abram receives a new name, many-nations promise, and land promise.

outline.heading: Eighth-day circumcision commanded
outline.note: The sign applies to every male in Abraham’s household.

outline.heading: Sarah and Isaac promised; Ishmael blessed
outline.note: The two sons’ futures are differentiated.

outline.heading: The household obeys
outline.note: Abraham circumcises the males on the same day.

outline.heading: The ordinance applied to Israel
outline.note: Heavenly tablets, election language, and a warning against neglect close the chapter.

keyVerses.text: And God said: 'Yea, and Sarah also shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name Isaac, and I will establish My covenant with him, an everlasting covenant, and for his seed after him.
keyVerses.why: The chapter names Isaac as Sarah's future son and locates the covenant specifically in his line.

keyVerses.text: And Abraham did according as God had said unto him, and he took Ishmael his son, and all that were born in his house, and whom he had bought with his money, every male in his house, and circumcised the flesh of their foreskin.
keyVerses.why: The instruction moves immediately into the household's enacted practice, including Ishmael and other males.

questions.question: What changes when Abram becomes Abraham?
questions.answer: God gives him a new name while saying he will become the father of many nations and kings. In the same speech the covenant and land promise are reaffirmed for his descendants.

questions.question: What is the “token” of the covenant?
questions.answer: The word means a visible sign, here circumcision of male foreskins on the eighth day. The text treats the timing as part of the ordinance, not as an incidental detail.

questions.question: Why are purchased males included in the circumcision rule?
questions.answer: The command includes males born in Abraham’s house and males bought from outsiders, and the household scene says it was carried out. This reports a world in which people could be owned; it does not authorize ownership or erase the ethical difficulty of that setting.

questions.question: What does Abraham ask about Ishmael?
questions.answer: He asks that Ishmael live before God, and God responds with a blessing, many descendants, and twelve princes. The chapter nevertheless says the named covenant will be established with Isaac, Sarah’s promised son.

questions.question: Does Isaac’s election mean Ishmael receives no blessing?
questions.answer: No. The speech explicitly blesses Ishmael and predicts a large nation while distinguishing the covenant line of Isaac. The later verses also use sharper exclusionary language, which should be read as this work’s theological claim rather than a verdict on any living people.

questions.question: Why does the passage mention angels when discussing circumcision?
questions.answer: Verse 27 portrays the angels of the presence and sanctification as created in the circumcised condition, making them a heavenly model for Israel’s covenant sign. It does not narrate a circumcision procedure performed on angels; the claim concerns their condition from creation and Israel’s holiness alongside them.

questions.question: What is the warning about future neglect of the eighth day?
questions.answer: The angel predicts that some Israelites will leave sons uncircumcised and describes this as abandoning the covenant. The severe threatened judgment is part of this ancient community rule and does not confer present-day enforcement authority on readers.

questions.question: How does this chapter continue the childlessness problem?
questions.answer: Chapter 14 ended with Ishmael’s birth through Hagar, but Sarah had not yet borne a child. Here God explicitly promises Sarah a son, gives his name as Isaac, and fixes his birth for the following year.

glossary.def: The bodily covenant sign commanded here for males on the eighth day.
A standing rule or command, used here for the covenant sign across generations.
